title: Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks
authors: Shaoqing Ren, Kaiming He, Ross Girshick, Jian Sun

pages.title: The core idea
pages.subtitle: Let the network propose its own regions

blocks.html: The question this page answers: object detectors of 2014–2015 had gotten fast at classifying candidate boxes, but they were still slow because of how they found those candidate boxes in the first place. This paper removes that last bottleneck and makes detection nearly real-time.

The bottleneck, concretely. A detector must first guess where objects might be (region proposals), then decide what each region is. Fast R-CNN had made the ‘what’ step fast, but the ‘where’ step still used Selective Search, a hand-engineered algorithm that runs on the CPU and takes about 2 seconds per image. The detection network itself ran in well under a second — so the system spent most of its wall-clock time waiting for proposals it could not parallelize on the GPU.

The insight. The convolutional feature map the detector already computes over the whole image contains everything needed to guess where objects are. So why compute proposals with a separate CPU algorithm? Faster R-CNN adds a tiny Region Proposal Network (RPN) that reads that same shared feature map and emits candidate boxes almost for free — in about 10 ms instead of 2 seconds.

An RPN is a fully convolutional network that simultaneously predicts object bounds and objectness scores at each position ... sharing their full-image convolutional features with the detection network, thus enabling nearly cost-free region proposals.

The payoff, in numbers. The unified detector runs at 5 fps with the deep VGG-16 backbone (and ~17 fps with the small ZF backbone) while setting state-of-the-art accuracy: about 73.2% mAP on PASCAL VOC 2007 and 70.4% mAP on VOC 2012, plus strong COCO numbers. (mAP, ‘mean Average Precision,’ averages detection precision across all object classes — the standard detection score.)

Why it mattered. Faster R-CNN became the template for two-stage detection for years, and its anchor mechanism became shared vocabulary reused by SSD, RetinaNet, YOLOv2+, and many others. It was also the detection framework that ResNet plugged into to sweep the 2015 ImageNet/COCO challenges, and the baseline DETR later defined itself against.

pages.title: From R-CNN to the proposal bottleneck
pages.subtitle: Where the time went

blocks.html: The lineage. The R-CNN family detects in two stages: (1) propose regions that might contain an object, then (2) classify each region and refine its box. Understanding why proposals became the bottleneck means tracing three generations.

items: R-CNN (2014): ~2000 Selective Search proposals per image, each cropped and pushed through a CNN separately. Accurate but glacial — tens of seconds per image — because the CNN ran 2000 times.
Fast R-CNN (2015): run the CNN once over the whole image, then pool features per proposal from the shared feature map (RoI pooling). The classify step dropped to a fraction of a second — a huge win.
Remaining problem: Fast R-CNN still got its proposals from Selective Search on the CPU (~2 s), which now dominated runtime.

blocks.html: The tangible imbalance. Once Fast R-CNN made detection take ~0.2 s, the ~2 s of Selective Search meant the system was idle ~90% of the time waiting for a non-GPU algorithm. Speeding up the detector further was pointless until the proposal step moved onto the GPU and shared work with the detector.

The key observation. The shared convolutional feature map computed for detection already encodes where objects likely are. Faster R-CNN bolts a small proposal network directly onto that feature map, turning two separate systems into one network with two heads — an RPN head that proposes and a Fast R-CNN head that classifies and refines. Proposals now cost ~10 ms and the whole thing trains and runs as a single GPU model.

Trivia. All four authors — Shaoqing Ren, Kaiming He, Ross Girshick, Jian Sun — are detection/CNN luminaries; Girshick authored R-CNN and Fast R-CNN, and He authored ResNet the same year. Faster R-CNN and ResNet were developed in the same lab and combined to win the 2015 challenges.

pages.title: The Region Proposal Network and anchors
pages.subtitle: A sliding window over shared features

blocks.html: What the RPN is. A small fully-convolutional network that slides over the shared feature map. At each spatial position it looks at an $n\times n$ window (the paper uses $n=3$), maps that window to a lower-dimensional vector (256-d for ZF, 512-d for VGG), and feeds it to two sibling output heads: a box-regression head and a box-classification (objectness) head that scores object-vs-background. Because it is convolutional, sliding the window is just a $3\times3$ conv applied across the whole map — one pass, no loop — which is why proposals are nearly free.

The problem anchors solve. Objects come in many sizes and shapes — a pencil, a person, a bus. A single box predicted per location could only commit to one shape. The fix is to attach, at every position, a set of reference boxes of different sizes and aspect ratios called anchors. The RPN then predicts, for each anchor, (a) how likely it contains an object and (b) small adjustments to make it fit better.

A concrete anchor. The default design uses 3 scales × 3 aspect ratios = 9 anchors per position. The scales cover small/medium/large objects (areas like 128², 256², 512² pixels) and the ratios cover tall/square/wide shapes (1:2, 1:1, 2:1). So at one location the RPN can simultaneously consider a tall thin box, a wide flat box, and a square box at three sizes — nine guesses — and score each.

items: Anchors give translation-invariant, multi-scale references — no need for an image pyramid or a pyramid of differently-sized filters, which is what made earlier multi-scale detectors slow.
Classification head: outputs 2 scores per anchor (object vs. background), so $2k$ scores where $k=9$ anchors.
Regression head: outputs 4 coordinate offsets per anchor, so $4k$ numbers.
For a $W\times H$ feature map there are $W\cdot H\cdot 9$ anchors total — on the order of ~20,000 for a typical image.

blocks.html: The box parameterization. The RPN does not predict absolute pixel coordinates; it predicts offsets relative to its anchor. For predicted center $(x,y)$, size $(w,h)$, anchor $(x_a,y_a,w_a,h_a)$, the targets are $t_x=(x-x_a)/w_a$, $t_y=(y-y_a)/h_a$, $t_w=\log(w/w_a)$, $t_h=\log(h/h_a)$. Dividing by the anchor size makes the targets scale-normalized, and the $\log$ on width/height keeps them small and symmetric — both make the regression well-conditioned and easy to learn.

Design rationale. Regressing offsets from good reference boxes is far easier than predicting boxes from scratch (the targets are small and centered), and decoupling the boxes from the feature map’s resolution lets one feature map cover all object sizes at once — the single trick that makes the RPN both fast and accurate.

pages.title: Training the detector
pages.subtitle: A multi-task loss and shared features

blocks.html: Labeling the anchors. Each anchor is labeled by its overlap with the ground-truth boxes, measured by IoU (Intersection-over-Union: the area of overlap divided by the area of union, between 0 and 1). An anchor is positive if its IoU with some ground-truth box exceeds 0.7 (or it is the best-matching anchor for that box), and negative if its IoU with every box is below 0.3. Anchors in between are ignored. Each mini-batch samples ~256 anchors from one image, kept near a 1:1 positive:negative ratio so the abundant background does not swamp training.
The multi-task loss. The RPN learns objectness and box refinement jointly:

blocks.tex: L(\{p_i\}, \{t_i\}) = \frac{1}{N_{cls}} \sum_i L_{cls}(p_i, p_i^*) + \lambda \frac{1}{N_{reg}} \sum_i p_i^* L_{reg}(t_i, t_i^*)

blocks.html: Reading it term by term. $i$ indexes anchors in the mini-batch. $p_i$ is the predicted probability anchor $i$ is an object; $p_i^*$ is its ground-truth label (1 if positive, 0 if negative). $t_i$ is the 4-vector of predicted box offsets and $t_i^*$ the ground-truth offsets (from the parameterization on the previous page). $L_{cls}$ is the log loss over the two classes (object / not). $L_{reg}$ is a smooth-L1 (Huber) loss on the box offsets — robust to outliers, unlike plain L2. $N_{cls}$ and $N_{reg}$ normalize the two terms (by the batch size and the number of anchor locations), and $\lambda$ (set so the two terms are roughly balanced) weights regression against classification.

The crucial $p_i^*$ factor. Note the regression term is multiplied by $p_i^*$. Since $p_i^*=0$ for negative anchors, the box-regression loss is active only for positive anchors — we only learn to refine boxes that actually contain an object, because ‘the right box for a patch of background’ is meaningless.

Sharing features between the two heads. The RPN and the Fast R-CNN detector are made to share the same convolutional backbone rather than each learning its own — otherwise the ‘nearly free’ benefit would be lost. The paper trains this with a 4-step alternating optimization: train the RPN; train Fast R-CNN on the RPN’s proposals; re-train the RPN with the shared conv layers frozen; finally fine-tune the detector head. A later approximate-joint scheme trains both in one pass. The detector then takes the top-scoring RPN proposals, RoI-pools each from the shared map, and outputs the final class label and refined box.

The headline result. Replacing Selective Search with the RPN both speeds up detection and improves accuracy — you rarely get both at once. The learned, detection-aware proposals turn out to be better than the generic hand-engineered ones, because they are trained end-to-end on the same features the detector uses.
The accuracy. On PASCAL VOC 2007 the system reaches about 73.2% mAP, and on VOC 2012 about 70.4% mAP — state of the art at the time, beating the Selective-Search-based Fast R-CNN it replaced.

Reading the trade-off. The lightweight ZF backbone runs at 17 fps but is less accurate; the heavier VGG-16 backbone runs at 5 fps with much higher mAP. Either way, proposal generation drops from ~2 seconds (Selective Search) to about 10 ms — a ~200× speedup on that stage, which is the entire reason the system can approach real time.

Why shared features are the secret. Because the RPN and detector reuse the same backbone, the only extra cost over a single forward pass is the tiny RPN head and the RoI pooling. The proposal step is no longer a separate program on the CPU but a few convolutions on the GPU, riding for free on features the detector needed anyway.

Quality over quantity. The most telling ablation: how many proposals do you need to find all the objects? Selective Search needs ~2000 proposals per image to reach high recall; the RPN matches or beats that recall with only ~300 proposals, because its proposals are learned and therefore concentrated on real objects. Fewer proposals also means the downstream detector runs faster — a compounding win.

Generalizing to COCO. The RPN also transfers to the larger, harder MS COCO dataset (80 classes, ~330k images, stricter IoU-based evaluation), where Faster R-CNN posted strong numbers and formed the basis of competition-winning entries — notably when combined with the ResNet backbone soon after. The shared-feature design is precisely what makes scaling the backbone worthwhile: a better backbone improves both the proposals and the final classification at once.
For the very deep VGG-16 model, our detection system has a frame rate of 5 fps (including all steps) on a GPU, while achieving state-of-the-art object detection accuracy.

Ablation rationale. The authors verify each piece matters: sharing the conv features (vs. two separate networks) both speeds things up and lifts mAP; using multiple anchor scales/ratios beats using a single anchor shape; and tuning $\lambda$ in the loss has only a mild effect, showing the design is robust. Together these establish that the gains come from the architecture, not from incidental tuning.

The lasting template. Faster R-CNN defined the two-stage detector that dominated detection for years: a shared backbone, an RPN that proposes, and a head that classifies and refines. This decomposition — propose, then classify — with everything sharing one set of features became the default mental model for object detection.

The anchor legacy. The anchor mechanism it introduced — tiling reference boxes of multiple scales and ratios and regressing offsets from them — became standard vocabulary, reused by single-stage detectors (SSD, RetinaNet) and later YOLO versions. The subsequent move to ‘anchor-free’ detectors (FCOS, CornerNet) and to set-prediction detectors (DETR) was explicitly framed in contrast to Faster R-CNN’s anchors, which shows how central the idea became.

items: Introduced the Region Proposal Network, generating proposals from shared conv features in ~10 ms instead of ~2 s.
Introduced anchors (3 scales × 3 ratios = 9 per location) as translation-invariant, multi-scale references.
Unified proposal + detection into one trainable GPU network at 5–17 fps with state-of-the-art mAP (73.2% VOC07).
Became the backbone of countless detectors, the framework ResNet used to win the 2015 ImageNet/COCO challenges, and the baseline DETR later compared itself against.

blocks.html: Context & trivia. Faster R-CNN extended to instance segmentation as Mask R-CNN (2017, He et al.) by adding a mask-prediction head — a direct descendant that won the Marr Prize. The ‘5 fps’ in the title was ‘real-time enough’ for 2015; single-stage detectors like YOLO and SSD soon traded a little accuracy for much higher frame rates, defining the speed-vs-accuracy axis that still organizes the detection literature today.
